title: Small Moves That Help When Things Get Challenging
author: Marcus Luther
summary: Marcus Luther, a high school English teacher in his fifteenth year, describes October as the month when early-year enthusiasm meets rising workload and a wall of fatigue. He offers four practical moves: do not open negative non-urgent messages mid-lesson and reply the next day, counterbalance a stressful interaction with something positive such as notes home or thanks to a colleague, remove something from your plate even if it is good (he dropped a long-running mindmapping ritual), and return to your values by making them visible, including by asking students which core belief should be the priority. He admits that moves do not always work and that positivity can become toxic when deeper problems exist, so values are the most resilient lens. The post ends with a short list of recommended reading and listening.
points: Delay opening and answering non-urgent negative messages so the weight does not enter the classroom and your presence with students is protected.
Counterbalance a stressful interaction with a deliberate investment in something good, such as a positive note to a parent or celebrating a colleague.
Being good and meaningful is not enough to keep something on your plate; Luther cut a five-year ritual once his systems reached overload.
Making core values visible, even listing each student's top value on the roster, keeps a teacher aligned and invites students to hold you accountable.
Moves are not guaranteed, and counterbalancing can slip into toxic positivity, which is why values are the more resilient anchor.
quotes: One of the overwhelming parts of teaching is the constant straddling of being present with students all day and still navigating the various other responsibilities of the job—many of which show up in our world through digital can-show-up-out-of-nowhere messages that are just a click away.
The value of waiting to open it is rather straightforward: it allows you to stay present within the classroom with students that is a win for them just as much as it is a win for you.

Sometimes we do not have agency over the stressful or frustrating aspects of our work, but I do believe we have agency over how we continue to lean into what is good—including how we name and invest in the good we are seeing around us.

I recognize that all this accumulated good can become its own obstacle, though, when the label of “good and meaningful” prevents us from honestly assessing our capacity and removing something from our plates when necessary.

There are many types of burnout as a teacher, but I think the most pernicious is when you start losing grasp of what actually matters to you in this work—and for me the best way to hold myself accountable to my own values is to make them as visible as possible
Slowing down to respond to a difficult email does not eliminate the difficult email, not to mention that it isn’t necessarily the best habit to be consistently delaying email responses.
